newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Orbotech aims to keep sales momentum.
newsitem.headline: Orbotech aims to keep sales momentum.

text.p: Israel's Orbotech Ltd, riding high on surging demand for its printed circuit board inspection gear, is eyeing acquisitions to diversify its business and help to cover its huge global sales and service operation.

"We are looking at companies that have either market synergy or product synergy, and best of all both," executive vice president Dan Falk said, adding that he expected Orbotech would be announcing a major acquisition some time during 1997.

Orbotech has the resources to go hunting -- it was sitting on $43 million in cash at the end of the first quarter -- thanks to surging orders for its automated optical inspection (AOI) equipment used in making printed circuit boards (PCBs).

Sales of PCB-AOI systems, which comprise 79 percent of Orbotech's revenues, grew 24 percent in the first quarter from a year earlier. That pushed total revenue up 10 percent to $41.4 million, carrying net income 34 percent higher to $6.5 million, or $0.49 a share.

Demand for PCBs, which are found in almost every high tech product, has been growing sharply in tandem with the computer and telecommmunications industries. Technical advances in PCB design have also helped Orbotech sales by making the inspection process more critical and complicated.
"In the last three years half our sales have not been capacity-driven but technology-driven," said Falk. "We see a shift to much more sophisticated boards."

Building sales is critical for Orbotech because its products require an extensive support and service network. Falk said the company has 400 staff in 40 locations around the world that cost it $50 million annually.

Higher revenues entail only marginal increases in expenses, said Falk. That explains why Orbotech reported record gross margins in the first quarter of 49.8 percent, up from 47.1 percent for all of 1996 and just 38.5 percent in 1993.

But how long Orbotech can continue to rely on growing PCB-AOI sales is anyone's guess. The long-term outlook was strong, as advanced electronics found their way into new segments like automobiles, but there could be spikes along the way and market visibility was not long, Falk said.

Acquisitions are only one part of Orbotech's diversification and expansion strategy. The company is also developing new products for emerging markets in AOI devices used in manufacturing liquid crystal displays (LCD) and shadow masks, which are used inside cathode ray tubes.

Salomon Brothers analyst Victor Halpert estimates sales of Orbotech's LCD-AOI systems will grow to $12 million this year from $2.6 million in 1996 while shadow mask AOI devices will generate $10 million in sales in 1998 from $3 million this year.
LCDs promise to turn into a major new market as costs come down and they replace cathode ray tubes (CRTs) as the basic computer screen.
Orbotech would face stiffer competition in that segment, which is dominated by Japanese and South Korean manufacturers, than in PCB-AOI systems, Falk acknowledged.
Analysts estimate the company controls about 70 percent of the PCB-AOI equipment market, but in LCD-AOI systems Falk said Orbotech would be pitted against Japan's Acrotec, a unit of Japan Energy.
"They have a marketing advantage in being in Japan -- that's important," said Falk, adding that Orbotech had the technological lead.

Orbotech's stock price has tracked the company's rising fortunes. In the last seven months, it has risen more than 150 percent to $29 7/8 in Nasdaq trading on Wednesday. The sharp run-up has caused Halpert to downgrade Orbotech to a buy from a strong buy, even though he remains keen on the company.

But Ted Kundtz, an analyst at Lehman Brothers in New York, said Orbotech's share price still had a lot of upside. He is looking at earnings per share (EPS) growing to $1.99 this year and $2.35 in 1998 from a $1.54 in 1996. That means Orbotech is trading an attractive 15 times 1997 EPS and 12.8 times 1998 EPS.
"There's a lot of momentum in the core business and we think the new product areas are coming in as anticipated," said Kundtz. "The stock is still very reasonably priced."
